summary: Weekly POC sync focused on Dedicated sizing and autoscaling policies. Reviewed last week's benchmark results (baseline + burst), discussed tradeoffs for burst capacity vs reserved baseline, clarified 95th pct latency SLOs, outlined next benchmark (500 concurrent burst), and agreed on action items: share sizing spreadsheet, upload traffic shape, deliver autoscale YAML examples, and send security docs.
topics: Fallbacks to hosted variants / graceful degradation
transcript: 00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check we all good on audio?
00:06 Evan: yeah all good, thanks Jordan, excited to go through the numbers
00:12 Maya: cool, i'll kick off with the summary of last week's runs, heads up some of the auto-transcript text is messy
00:20 Maya: so run one was reserved baseline at 120 rps, p50 p95 p99 were roughly 45, 160, 320 ms respectively, token cost looked inline with our proforma
00:36 Sofia: can i pause — 120 rps baseline is what we agreed, right? our spike patterns go to 500 for short bursts
00:42 Jordan: correct, and that's the focus — how to handle 500 req bursts without reserving huge capacity always
01:00 Maya: for the burst test we did two modes: pre-warm reserved and autoscale-with-burst, pre-warm hit the 95th at ~200 ms, autoscale had a cold-start tail that went to ~1.2s on a few requests
01:20 Liam: that cold-start tail is the main risk for UX; can we mitigate?
01:28 Maya: yes, options: keep a small buffer pool (warm instances), aggressive prefetch of KV cache, or use a short-lived dedicated burst pool with warmup hooks. each has cost tradeoffs
01:46 Evan: are these warm pools something Redwood offers in Dedicated?

01:50 Jordan: yep, we can configure reserved baseline + burst pool. autoscaling policy supports minimums, scale step sizes, and a burst reserve that can be billed differently — we'll send an example YAML
02:10 Sofia: also curious about graceful degradation — if we hit capacity can we fallback to a smaller model or to hosted endpoint?

02:18 Maya: yes, smart routing supports fallback to a smaller quantized variant or to hosted Redwood API. you can set policy priorities: region, cost tier, and model rank. there were a few words mis-transcribed earlier re: "kv cache" as "kay vee cash"
02:42 Evan: nice — for sensitive data we need VPC + KMS, any differences in behavior for those modes?
02:48 Jordan: no difference functionally; private deployments just change networking and key mgmt. audit logs and token-level tracing remain available in console
03:00 Liam: what's the SLA we can expect on Dedicated? 99.9?
03:04 Jordan: standard Dedicated SLA is 99.9 with burst policies tuned for latency SLOs — we can scope a bespoke SLA in enterprise contract
03:18 Maya: back to numbers — cost delta for keeping a 20% buffer of GPUs vs relying on instant autoscale was about 18% higher in monthly run-rate but reduced p99 tail significantly
03:34 Evan: can you quantify p99 improvement?
03:38 Maya: p99 went from 1.1s to ~380ms when buffer was kept warm in our test workload (which has lookahead-friendly KV cache patterns)
03:54 Sofia: so tradeoff is extra cost vs user-facing latency. our product team is very sensitive to p95 but also p99 for pageloads
04:06 Jordan: action item — we'll put these scenarios in the sizing spreadsheet with cost and latency columns so you can pick the right point on the curve
04:14 Evan: great, also wanted to confirm the burst billing model — is burst billed at on-demand rates or a special rate?
04:20 Jordan: typically burst is billed at a slightly higher on-demand rate; reserved committed capacity gets discounted pricing. we'll reflect both in the spreadsheet
04:32 Maya: note: in the auto-scaler there are knobs like scale_cooldown, scale_step, and target_utilization. we recommended conservative step sizes to avoid flapping during quick spikes
04:46 Evan: can you show recommended values?
04:50 Maya: yes — recommended starting point in our environment: min_instances = 2, max_instances = 12, scale_step = 2, cooldown = 60s, target_utilization = 0.65. i'll include Yaml snippet
05:06 Liam: curious about burst warmup time — how long to spin a new instance and warm kv cache?
05:12 Maya: spin-up is about 20-30s for the binary on GPU, kv cache warm depends on prefix patterns; for many chat flows warmup can be 5-10 requests per instance to reach stable latencies
05:28 Evan: ok, so for a 10 minute burst that spikes to 500, autoscale alone may not prevent some cold-start tail — sounds like we should plan for a small warm buffer
05:38 Jordan: agreed — plan is baseline reserved to cover 60-70% of typical peak, plus a small warm pool sized for expected burst concurrency, and autoscale for beyond that
06:00 Sofia: quick security Q — do you support customer-managed KMS for key rotation?
06:06 Jordan: yes, we support KMS/HSM integrations and customer-managed keys for private deployments. we'll share the security checklist
06:18 Evan: perfect. one other ask from our infra team: can we test failover to hosted Redwood if a region loses capacity?

06:26 Maya: yes, multi-region fallback can be configured with health checks and prioritized routing. the failover will respect privacy settings but we should walk through data residency constraints first
06:40 Liam: scope for the next benchmark — can Redwood set up a 10 minute window to reproduce a 500 concurrent burst with our traffic shape?
06:46 Jordan: yes, we'll schedule it, jordan: i'll coordinate via shared calendar and include test creds
06:54 Evan: and we'll provide traffic shape CSV by EOD Wednesday
07:00 Maya: noted, and then we'll run with three configs: baseline reserved, reserved+warm-buffer, and autoscale-only to show delta
07:10 Sofia: will you capture token-level cost per config? that helps procurement
07:14 Maya: yes cost per 1k tokens and per-hour GPU cost will be logged, we'll add to spreadsheet
07:22 Evan: any notes on quantization impacts on latency and quality?
07:26 Maya: quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput; quality impact varies by model and prompt, we'll include a quick eval on your sample prompts as part of the run
07:40 Jordan: quick status check — SOC2 and ISO questions? Liam?
07:44 Liam: we need SOC2 type II and evidence of audit logging, also SSO via SAML, and RBAC for team ops
07:52 Jordan: yes on all three, we'll send SOC2 package and mappings for SSO/RBAC, expect that in the security docs packet
08:02 Evan: any blockers on your side for the benchmark?
08:06 Maya: just the traffic shape and target SLO, and we need permission to run load from our test accounts
08:12 Evan: we'll grant test accounts and send csv
08:16 Jordan: awesome — next steps recap then: Maya to share autoscale YAML and sizing spreadsheet, Evan to provide traffic csv and SLO, Jordan to schedule burst run and provide creds
08:28 Sofia: can you include an example of fallback policy that routes to a smaller model if latency exceeds threshold?
08:34 Maya: yes, we have a sample policy that switches model variants at runtime based on latency percentiles, will add that
08:40 Evan: last Q — any gotchas for quantized model cold starts and KV caches?
08:44 Maya: quantized weights load slightly faster but KV cache priming still dominates first requests, so warm buffers help there too
08:56 Jordan: okay folks, thanks, we'll aim to run the benchmark next Tuesday during your window unless you prefer earlier
09:02 Evan: tuesday works, i'll confirm offline
09:06 Jordan: great. we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and security docs after the call, thanks everyone
09:12 (end of recording)
